title: How To Survive The Politics Of Another Covid School Year
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Writing amid ongoing pandemic-era political division among parents, colleagues, and students, Linsin offers a three-part approach for teachers to protect their own wellbeing without becoming entangled in the conflict. 'Be okay' means accepting that colleagues, parents, and students will hold differing views on mandates and vaccines without needing to change anyone's mind or feel anger toward them. 'Be accepting' means working through proper channels to influence policy while on personal time, but accepting everything that can't be changed while on the clock, refocusing on the core purpose of serving students rather than being right. 'Be quiet' means declining to share personal opinions on divisive topics at school, saving those conversations for outside of work, on the grounds that engaging invites stress and can gradually distort one's view of people who think differently. He closes by warning that unchecked anxiety over politics can erode empathy and relationships, and urges teachers to model calm, grace, and professionalism instead.
points: A three-part framework — 'be okay,' 'be accepting,' 'be quiet' — is offered to help teachers navigate pandemic-era political division without personal burnout.
Teachers are urged to accept differing views on masks and vaccines among colleagues, parents, and students without needing to change anyone's mind.
Advocacy for change should happen through proper channels (school board meetings, running for office) on personal time, not on the job.
Declining to share personal opinions on divisive topics at school is framed as protecting both stress levels and professional relationships.
Unchecked political anxiety is described as capable of eroding empathy and hardening one's view of people who think differently.
quotes: Wild-eyed parents . Petrified students. Bat-crazy colleagues. Changing policies. Uncertainties. Obstacles. Frustrations. STRESS.
It’s your attitude. Get it right by focusing on just three things , and you’ll float above the fray, untouchable, like a bird on the wing.
Be okay with others obnoxiously, and sometimes aggressively, trying to push their beliefs on the rest of the world.
If you want to change something, then go through the proper channels. Show up to school board meetings, run for office, or gather and protest to your heart’s content.
People who are comfortable in their own skin don’t take disagreement personally. They’re strong enough in their beliefs to not have to share them with the world or feel the need to change others.
Reorient toward acceptance, calmness, and quietude. Stop scattering seeds of division and instead take the road less traveled by being an exemplar of teaching excellence and professionalism.
